1000016.etyen:
The traditional European biblical form was transmitted through Latin Israel (“Israel”), from Ancient Greek Ἰσραήλ (Israḗl, “Israel”), from Biblical Hebrew יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yiśrāʾēl, “Israel”).
In the Bible, the name is given to the patriarch Jacob after he wrestles with God. It was subsequently applied to his descendants, the Israelite people, and their land; the modern state, established in 1948, took its name from this biblical usage. The Hebrew name has traditionally been interpreted as “God strives, fights” or “God rules”.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Israel, Danish Israel, Swedish Israel, German

en.g: a surname transferred from the place name, originating from one of several farms named Djupevik or Djupvik, particularly in southwestern Norway

1004368.etyen:
A Danicised form of the Norwegian farm name Djupevik, found in several places in Norway.
The place name continues Old Norse Djúpavík, from djúpr (“deep”) + vík (“bay, inlet”). Depending on the locality, the name could refer specifically to a bay extending deeply inland rather than to deep water. The surname is therefore habitational, originally denoting someone from a farm named Djupevik or Djupvik. Doublet of Gjøvik, Djupvik, and Dybvik.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Dybevik (“surname”).

1004880.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse *Álasund, from áll (“eel”) or áll (“stripe; channel”) and sund (“sound, strait”); the modern name has the neuter definite singular ending -et.
By surface analysis, Ålesund (“Ålesund”) + -et (“neuter definite singular ending”).
The name originally denoted the sound itself and was later transferred to the settlement as Ålesund.
Compare the corresponding Nynorsk Norwegian Nynorsk Ålesund (definite Ålesundet), Faroese Álasund and Icelandic Álasund.

en.g: congratulation; the act or an instance of congratulating someone
x: Etter premieutdelingen var det tid for klemmer og gratulering.
After the award ceremony, it was time for hugs and congratulations.
Og tusen takk for alle gratuleringene
And many thanks for all the congratulations

1005136.etyen:
From gratulere (“to congratulate”) + -ing (“action-noun-forming suffix”).
The verb ultimately derives from Latin grātulārī (“to congratulate”), formed from Latin grātus (“pleasing, welcome; grateful”), from Proto-Italic *gʷrātos (“grateful”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷr̥Htós (“praised”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH- (“to welcome, praise”). The suffix continues Old Norse -ing (“action-noun-forming suffix”), from Proto-Germanic *-ingō (“action-noun-forming suffix”).
Compare the parallel formation Norwegian Nynorsk gratulering (“congratulation; the act of congratulating”).
